subject: film
title: French New Wave (c. 1958–64): the camera leaves the studio
dek: Young French critics attacked the polished studio cinema they called the tradition of quality, then made their own films in real streets with lighter cameras. A 1959–62 burst of features, and a magazine that had already trained an audience, gave the press a name: Nouvelle Vague.

thumb.alt: Agnès Varda standing on a wooden structure over water, early 1960s.

hero.alt: Rue Soufflot in Paris looking toward the Panthéon, late 1950s, with pedestrians and parked cars.
hero.caption: Rue Soufflot, looking toward the Panthéon, around the end of the 1950s. New Wave films treated streets like this as the set: available light, real traffic, a city that did not have to be rebuilt on a soundstage.

honesty: “Nouvelle Vague” was a press label before it was a school. The people in this lesson argued in Cahiers du Cinéma, learned at the Cinémathèque as much as at the official film school IDHEC, then made films that did not look like the tradition de qualité they had been attacking. This lesson looks out from Paris. Free Cinema, the Japanese New Wave, and cinéma vérité were happening in the same years. They are not assigned peers. Taiwan New Cinema is a later relative that borrowed the “new cinema” idea, not a 1960 contemporary.

timeline.label: Cahiers
timeline.detail: Cahiers du Cinéma was founded in 1951. Truffaut’s 1954 essay “Une certaine tendance du cinéma français” named the tradition de qualité as the enemy.

timeline.label: Before the name
timeline.detail: Varda’s La Pointe Courte and Chabrol’s Le Beau Serge. Critics were already picking up cameras before the press had a label for them.

timeline.label: Cannes
timeline.detail: Les Quatre Cents Coups and Hiroshima mon amour. The festival gave international journalists a date they could print.

timeline.label: The burst
timeline.detail: À bout de souffle, Paris nous appartient, Lola, Jules et Jim, and Cléo de 5 à 7 arrived in a short stretch of years.

timeline.label: Elsewhere
timeline.detail: Free Cinema and the British New Wave; the Japanese New Wave; cinéma vérité. Same years, different arguments with their own studios.

timeline.label: A later relative
timeline.detail: Taiwan New Cinema. The French name traveled. Travel is not the same as origin.

glossary.explain: Press name, late 1950s, for a cluster of mostly young French directors who had often been critics first. A useful label, and a bad census of everyone who was making films that way.
Truffaut’s hostile name for the polished, literary, studio-bound French cinema of the 1940s–50s that Cahiers wanted to replace. “Quality” here is an insult.
Postwar French film societies that screened and argued over films outside the commercial circuit. A training ground before a camera was a job.
The official French film school (Institut des hautes études cinématographiques). The New Wave’s joke was that you could learn more in the dark at the Cinémathèque than in its classrooms.
The Cinémathèque française, the archive and screening room associated with Henri Langlois. For the Cahiers critics it was a school: Hollywood and Europe, night after night.
Co-founder of the Cinémathèque française. The programmers’ programmer: he showed the films the school and the industry had filed as disposable.
Critic and co-founder of Cahiers du Cinéma. A father figure the younger writers both used and argued with.
French film magazine, founded 1951. Truffaut, Godard, Chabrol, Rivette, and Rohmer wrote there. The magazine trained an audience and then supplied directors.

Cahiers argument: a director can be the author of a film the way a novelist is the author of a book — including in Hollywood, if the films have a signature. In English this hardened into “auteur theory.” It was a polemic, not a law of nature.
The director-as-author, in the Cahiers sense. A fighting word before it was a festival brochure word.
Hollywood director the Cahiers critics treated as an author, not a genre mechanic. The insult to French “quality” was the point.
Hollywood director claimed by Cahiers as an auteur. Hawks, Hitchcock, Nicholas Ray: the American names in the French fight.
Hollywood director (Rebel Without a Cause and others) whom Cahiers treated as a signature, not a studio employee.
An edit that skips a bit of time inside a continuous shot, so the image jerks. Breathless made the device famous as style, not as a mistake to be hidden.
Lightweight French 35mm camera (Éclair). New Wave crews used cameras like this because they could leave the studio.
Shooting with the light already in the street or room, rather than a studio grid. An aesthetic with a budget attached.
Filming in real streets and rooms instead of sets. Italian neorealism had already done this; Paris made it look like a choice and a generation.
Later grouping of filmmakers including Varda, Resnais, and Marker — often more essayistic than the Cahiers men. Useful as a map, and too neat if you treat it as a wall.
Producer of Breathless and other early New Wave features. The movement had a checkbook, not only a manifesto.
Producer who backed several New Wave and Left Bank films. Another name for the fact that cheap was not free.
Critic, then director. “Une certaine tendance du cinéma français” (1954); Les Quatre Cents Coups (1959). The man who attacked the tradition of quality later became, himself, a kind of tradition.
Critic, then director. À bout de souffle (1960) is the film people mean when they say “jump cut.” The longer fact is a director who treated cinema as an argument.
Cahiers critic, then director. Le Beau Serge (1958) is often called the first New Wave feature — a provincial story, not a Paris postcard.
Cahiers critic, then director. Paris nous appartient (1961) is a Paris of plots and rooms, longer-breathed than the jump-cut cliché.
Cahiers critic and later editor, then director of talkative moral tales. In the 1959–62 burst he is already in the magazine’s inner room.
Photographer first, then filmmaker. La Pointe Courte (1955) is often called a New Wave film before the name. Cléo de 5 à 7 (1962) is the later public proof she was not a guest.
Left Bank director. Hiroshima mon amour (1959) is a literary, time-tangled film from the same Cannes season as The 400 Blows — not a Cahiers boys’ night out.
Essay-filmmaker of the Left Bank. A name on the map even when a given year’s famous titles are someone else’s.
Director of Lola (1961). A musical intelligence in the same years; often parked beside Varda, which is geography and a marriage, not a full account.
Director of Les Amants (1958). Adjacent to the burst: a scandal about adult desire, not a Cahiers calling card.
Actor; Antoine Doinel in Les Quatre Cents Coups and later Truffaut films. A new face who became a recurring one.
American actress; the American in Paris in À bout de souffle. Breathless without her face is a different object.
Actor; the petty criminal in À bout de souffle. A new star who looked like he had walked in from the street.
Actress and Godard’s collaborator in the films just after Breathless. A face the New Wave kept walking back to.
Cinematographer of Breathless, Jules et Jim, and many other New Wave films. Handheld, available light, a camera that could walk.
Editor of Breathless. The jump cuts are hers as well as Godard’s.
Novelist and screenwriter of Hiroshima mon amour. The literary half of a film the Cahiers story likes to file under directors only.
The boy in Les Quatre Cents Coups, played by Jean-Pierre Léaud. Truffaut returned to him. A character, not a mascot.

glossary.term: Une certaine tendance du cinéma français
glossary.explain: Truffaut’s 1954 Cahiers essay attacking the tradition of quality. A fight about scripts, adaptation, and who authors a film.
Chabrol, 1958. Often cited as the first New Wave feature: a return to a provincial town, shot away from the studio comfort the essay had mocked.
Truffaut, 1959. Cannes made it an international event. Antoine Doinel in a Paris that is not a postcard.
Godard, 1960. Jump cuts, handheld, a thin crime plot. The event is the grammar.
Varda, 1962. A singer walks through two real-time hours of Paris while she waits for a medical result.
Resnais, 1959, screenplay by Duras. A French actress and a Japanese man; time that will not stay in order. Cannes, the same season as The 400 Blows.
Truffaut, 1962. A triangle, a stretch of the century, a camera that keeps moving. The film that made the New Wave look like it could also be tender and long.
Rivette, 1961. Conspiracy and rehearsal in a city that will not explain itself.
Demy, 1961. Nantes, a dancer, a musical pulse without yet being a full musical. Often parked beside Varda, which is geography and a marriage, not a full account of the film.
Malle, 1958. A bourgeois adultery film that became a censorship fight. Next to the New Wave, not inside its magazine.
Varda, 1955. A fishing village and a marriage, often called a New Wave film before the name existed.
British mid-1950s documentary movement (Anderson, Reisz, Richardson and others): short films, everyday subjects, a manifesto. Contemporaneous, not a French export.
British late-1950s/early-1960s features that grew out of Free Cinema and the kitchen-sink plays: working-class rooms, location shooting, a different class accent.
British Free Cinema and later feature director. A name on the British side of the same years.
British Free Cinema and New Wave director.
British Free Cinema and New Wave director.
Japanese 1960s directors (Oshima, Imamura, Teshigahara and others) breaking with studio form. The name borrows the French phrase. The films do not.
Japanese New Wave director. Cruel Story of Youth (1960) is the usual first citation in a short list.
Japanese New Wave director. Pigs and Battleships (1961) is one place the studio system starts to look breakable.
Japanese New Wave director. Woman in the Dunes (1964) is the international title people remember.
A documentary idea of the same years: lightweight cameras, direct sound, people talking in the present. Chronicle of a Summer (Rouch and Morin, 1961) is the usual French exhibit.
Anthropologist-filmmaker; with Edgar Morin, Chronicle of a Summer (1961). Cinéma vérité’s most cited French name.
Sociologist; with Jean Rouch, Chronicle of a Summer.
Rouch and Morin, 1961 (Chronique d’un été). Paris people, a lightweight camera, the present tense as a method.
Postwar Italian films that took ruined streets as a set. The New Wave’s location habit has this earlier cousin.
The festival that, in 1959, made Les Quatre Cents Coups an international event. A prize is not a movement, but it is how a movement gets a date journalists can print.
U.S. late-1960s/1970s studio crash and youth-market turn. Bonnie and Clyde (1967) is the usual bridge sentence from the New Wave. A later effect, not a twin.
Arthur Penn, 1967. The sentence film histories use to connect Paris to New Hollywood. The connection is real and incomplete.
1980s Taiwanese film movement (Hou Hsiao-hsien, Edward Yang, and others). A later cousin in the family of “new cinemas,” not a 1960 contemporary.
Taiwan New Cinema director. A later name, for the after — not a 1959 peer.
Taiwan New Cinema director. Again: 1980s, a cousin, not a contemporary.

fun_fact.title: The jump cuts were also a way to shorten the film
fun_fact.text: Godard and editor Cécile Decugis shortened Breathless by cutting inside shots, not only between them. The jump cut is now taught as a philosophy of time. It was also a way to lose running time without reshooting Paris. Both things can be true: a device can be an idea and a solution to a reel that was too long.

sections.title: A fight with studio “quality,” a magazine, and a camera light enough to carry

blocks.text: The French cinema the young critics wanted to replace had a name they gave it: tradition de qualité, or cinéma de qualité — well-upholstered literary adaptations, studio craft, a finished look that felt, to them, dead. François Truffaut’s 1954 Cahiers du Cinéma essay “Une certaine tendance du cinéma français” is the fight in print. The other half of the fight was the politique des auteurs. A director, even in Hollywood, could be an author. Alfred Hitchcock counted. So did Howard Hawks. So did Nicholas Ray. The insult to the French studio system was the point: if those American directors were authors, the polished French adapters were not.

They had learned the argument in rooms that were not IDHEC, the official French film school. Postwar ciné-clubs trained an audience to argue. The Cinémathèque française, under Henri Langlois, showed Hollywood and Europe as if the distinction did not matter. André Bazin’s Cahiers, founded in 1951, hired the arguers: Truffaut, Jean-Luc Godard, Claude Chabrol, Jacques Rivette, Éric Rohmer. The official school existed. The joke — and it was only half a joke — was that you learned more in Langlois’s dark than in a curriculum.

blocks.alt: An Éclair Cameflex 35mm movie camera on a tripod, labeled Eclair Paris and Chevereau.
blocks.caption: An Éclair Cameflex, the kind of relatively light 35mm camera Paris rental houses such as Chevereau supplied. New Wave form is often taught as an idea. It is also equipment that could be carried into a street.

blocks.text: They were not the first people to want a camera outside. Italian neorealism had already taken the war’s rubble as a set. What was new in Paris was the combination: critics who became directors, a magazine that had already trained an audience, faster film stock, lighter cameras, and producers — Georges de Beauregard, Pierre Braunberger — willing to bet on a low budget that looked like a choice.

sections.title: What the films looked like once they left the studio

blocks.text: The look is easy to list and easy to turn into a costume. Location shooting. Jump cuts. Available light. Young non-stars or new faces: Jean-Pierre Léaud, Jean Seberg, Jean-Paul Belmondo, Anna Karina. Handheld cameras, Raoul Coutard walking them through traffic. A 1959–62 burst in which it suddenly seemed that everyone who had written for Cahiers, and several people who had not, had a feature. Left Bank versus the Cahiers group is a map of that burst, not a ranking: Varda, Alain Resnais, Chris Marker, Jacques Demy on one side of a useful line; Truffaut, Godard, Chabrol, Rivette, Rohmer on the other. Louis Malle’s Les Amants (1958) sits beside that cluster. The line leaks. That is why it is a map and not a membership list.

blocks.alt: Paris street toward the Panthéon, late 1950s.
blocks.caption: The Latin Quarter as a working street, not a back lot. New Wave location shooting made Paris look like a place people already lived — which is why the city in these films still feels like itself, and why a production still needed permits, light, and luck.

blocks.text: Chabrol’s Le Beau Serge (1958) is the film historians often call the first New Wave feature: a return to a provincial town, not a Champs-Élysées postcard. Rivette’s Paris nous appartient (1961) makes the city a rumor of plots and rehearsals. Demy’s Lola (1961) finds a musical pulse in Nantes. The press needed a date anyway. Cannes, 1959, supplied one.

sections.title: Many filmmakers, and three films to look at closely

blocks.text: Truffaut, Godard, Chabrol, Rivette, Rohmer, Varda, Resnais, Marker, Demy, Malle: that is already too many for a poster and too few for a census. Add the actors — Léaud, Seberg, Belmondo, Karina — and the people who made the images possible: Coutard, Cécile Decugis, Duras, Beauregard, Braunberger, Langlois, Bazin. Deepen only a few works, as examples inside the field.

Les Quatre Cents Coups is the public breakthrough. Truffaut, who had been banned from Cannes as a critic, arrived in 1959 as a director and won best director. The film follows Antoine Doinel, played by Jean-Pierre Léaud, through a Paris that is not a postcard — school, streets, a runaway, a freeze-frame on a beach. It is the date the press needed. It is not the first film in the cluster. It is the one that made the cluster visible abroad.

À bout de souffle is the film that made the jump cut famous as a choice, not a mistake. Godard, 1960; Belmondo and Seberg; Coutard’s camera; Decugis in the cutting room. The plot is a thin crime story. Time skips inside shots. The hero talks as if the audience were in the room. Later classrooms will call this a philosophy. It was also a way to shorten a film without reshooting Paris. Both things can be true.

Cléo de 5 à 7 and Hiroshima mon amour keep the map from collapsing into two men and a jump cut. Varda’s 1962 film walks a singer through two real-time hours of Paris while she waits for a medical result. Resnais’s 1959 film, from a Duras screenplay, refuses to let time stay put: a French actress, a Japanese man, a city that is not Paris. La Pointe Courte had already been Varda’s earlier claim, in 1955. If “auteur” only fits the Cahiers men, the word is too small.

blocks.alt: Agnès Varda, short dark hair, standing with another woman on a wooden deck over water.
blocks.caption: Agnès Varda (left), early 1960s. The filename on this archive print says Venice, 1962 — the year of Cléo de 5 à 7. Treat the place-name as the archive’s label. The person is not in doubt: a director who was already working when the magazine men picked up cameras.

blocks.alt: Children looking through a professional motion-picture camera on a tripod, with an adult nearby.
blocks.caption: A later photograph of a portable camera on a tripod. This is not a 1959 production still. It is here because the New Wave’s bet — that a lighter camera changes who gets to shoot, and where — did not stay in Paris. The equipment traveled. The date of this picture is later than the era. The idea is the era’s.

blocks.text: In Britain, Free Cinema’s shorts and manifesto — Lindsay Anderson, Karel Reisz, Tony Richardson — had already argued for everyday subjects and a camera that did not owe the studio a polished lie. The British New Wave features that followed are contemporaneous, not a French franchise. In Japan, Nagisa Oshima, Shohei Imamura, Hiroshi Teshigahara and others were breaking studio form; the phrase nūberu bāgu borrows the French name and then goes its own way. Cinéma vérité — Jean Rouch and Edgar Morin’s Chronicle of a Summer (1961) — is another French argument of the same years: not fiction’s jump cut, but a claim on the present tense. These are contemporaneous arguments, not a ranking with France at the top.

sections.title: Later filmmakers borrowed the methods, and a later cinema borrowed the name

blocks.text: American studios in the late 1960s needed a younger audience and had lost the old Production Code’s certainty. Bonnie and Clyde (1967) is the sentence film histories use to connect Paris to New Hollywood. The connection is real and incomplete. A lot of other things — television, the draft, the collapse of the studio system’s weekly habit — were part of the same American turn.

Taiwan New Cinema, in the 1980s — Hou Hsiao-hsien, Edward Yang, and others — is sometimes filed as another “new wave.” It is a later relative: a different state, a different language politics, a different argument with its own studios. It does not belong on the 1958–64 timeline except as a reminder that the French name traveled, and that travel is not the same as origin.
If the director is the author, whose names have to wait in the credits?
